# Ring of Nestor

## Discovery and provenance

The Ring of Nestor is a large gold signet ring now in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, where it is catalogued as AN1938.1130 and described as a Late Minoan I signet ring dating broadly to about 1600–1450 BC. The ring entered the museum without a fully documented excavation context, and modern catalog summaries do not give a secure findspot. 

In 1925 Arthur J. Evans published a monograph titled “The ring of Nestor. A glimpse into the Minoan after-world and a sepulchral treasure of gold signet-rings and bead-seals from Thisbê, Boeotia,” in which he presented the ring as part of a “truly royal” funerary treasure of gold rings and bead seals said to have been found in a Mycenaean rock or chamber tomb near Thisbê in Boeotia, Greece. Evans reported that the treasure was discovered in 1915 by a peasant in a rock-cut chamber tomb near the village of Dombrena under wartime conditions, that the finds bypassed official archaeological channels, and that he could not reveal all details of the discovery without breaching confidences. His publication did not include an excavation plan, locus numbers, or stratigraphic documentation for the tomb, so the Boeotian association relies on narrative accounts rather than on formal excavation records. 

Later narratives sometimes place the ring in a Mycenaean funerary context near Pylos. A Pylos-focused publication describes the Ashmolean ring AN1938.1130 as a “chance find from here, the so-called Ring of Nestor,” associating it with the Pylos region but explicitly characterizing it as an uncontrolled discovery rather than a stratified excavation find. A. G. Vlachopoulos similarly states that the Ring of Nestor was “probably found in tholos A at Kakovatos,” linking it to a tholos tomb in Messenia while presenting this attribution as probable rather than certain. In the same discussion he distinguishes the ring from a group of gold rings “of known provenance” from Cretan sites, implying that the Ring of Nestor is not among the securely provenanced examples. 

Modern scholarship commonly treats the ring’s provenance as uncertain and classifies it among Aegean Bronze Age “dubitanda.” A Cambridge handbook chapter on “Fakes and Dubitanda” discusses the Ring of Nestor in a section on objects of doubtful authenticity and provenance, noting that alleged Boeotian, Pylian, or Cretan origins rest on dealers’ or collectors’ stories rather than on documented excavations. Hudler’s study of gemmae dubitandae likewise cites the Ring of Nestor as an example of a seal object whose archaeological properties and provenance are unknown or compromised and explicitly labels it a gemma dubitanda. These studies emphasize that there is no secure excavation or archival evidence confirming a specific findspot for the ring in Boeotia, Pylos, or Crete. 

Public descriptions sometimes state or imply a Cretan origin on stylistic grounds. A Facebook post, for example, calls the object “a ~3700-year-old gold signet ring from Crete, Late Minoan Period, (c. 1700–1450 BCE), now housed at the Ashmolean Museum,” but does not cite archaeological evidence for a Cretan findspot. Scholarly treatments distinguish such popular claims from secure provenance, stressing that stylistic classification as a Minoan or Minoan-style work does not by itself establish a Cretan excavation origin. 

## Description

The Ring of Nestor is a gold signet ring with an elliptical bezel measuring approximately 3.29 × 2.18 cm and weighing about 31.7–31.8 g, making it one of the largest known Aegean gold signet rings. The hoop’s inner diameter is recorded as about 1.4–1.56 cm and the band as roughly 0.82 × 0.35 cm. Ingo Pini gives the bezel’s long axis as 3.27 cm, a value very close to the Ashmolean and CMS figure of 3.29 cm. 

Ashmolean and related catalog records identify the ring as a gold signet with four cult scenes engraved on the bezel; a Heritage Images entry based on Ashmolean data describes it as a Late Minoan I signet ring with “four cult scenes.” Pinterest and other secondary summaries echo these descriptions, noting a weight around 31.8 g and the presence of four ritual or cult scenes on the bezel. 

Vlachopoulos observes that the imagery on the elliptical bezel can be divided into four main zones or scenes, separated not by incised frames but by the natural arrangement of figures and empty spaces. He describes one principal scene showing a seated figure, usually regarded as a female divinity or mistress, enthroned within a sanctuary-like setting defined by a base and columnar elements and accompanied by one or more griffins. Another zone shows a male figure approaching or gesturing toward a ship around which birds or spiritual beings appear, a configuration some scholars have interpreted as a sacred sea journey or voyage of the dead. A further scene depicts a figure walking or offering in front of a sacred tree or plant set against a rocky or mountainous background, forming a typical “sacred mountain/sacred tree” combination and miniature sacred landscape. 

A detailed iconographic study emphasizes that the ring’s repertoire of motifs—the mountainous background, sacred tree, altar or architectural elements, and griffin-like guardian beasts—closely parallels scenes on other Late Minoan I gold rings and wall paintings, indicating that these elements belong to a broader Aegean religious iconographic system. In this interpretation the griffins flanking the throne function as guardian or attendant animals rather than as protagonists in an independent narrative. 

Technical examinations highlight the craftsmanship of the engraving. Vlachopoulos notes that the lines are deeply cut, with multiple strokes enhancing contours, and that the rendering of faces, eyes, hair, garments, and musculature is detailed and comparable to Late Minoan I gold rings from Crete and Mycenae. Microscopic study reports moderate wear within the grooves and natural polishing, interpreted as indicating prolonged use or wear rather than superficial artificial ageing. Another iconographic and technical study points out that in areas such as shoulders, hips, and knees the figures’ outlines use broken or interrupted contour lines similar to securely genuine Minoan intaglios, contrasting with the smooth, even lines typical of many early twentieth-century forgeries. 

## Dating and cultural context

Museum and catalog entries classify the Ring of Nestor as a Late Minoan I gold signet ring, with date ranges around 1600–1450 BC or, more broadly, within the Late Minoan period. Pini assigns it to Late Minoan IB–II, corresponding approximately to 1530–1400 BC, and uses it as a representative of large gold signet rings of this phase. Non-academic summaries such as Pinterest pins sometimes give a wider Late Minoan range of about 1700–1450 BC. 

The dating is based on stylistic comparison and technological analysis rather than on stratified archaeological context. Pini’s overview of Minoan glyptic notes that the ring’s dimensions and complex religious composition align with a tendency in Late Minoan I–II for gold rings to adopt monumental scale and densely populated imagery. Vlachopoulos situates the ring within a corpus of Late Minoan I gold rings characterized by deep, multi-stroke intaglio carving and iconography centered on sacred landscapes, divinities, ships, and winged creatures. A study on “Traces of Places” describes the Ring of Nestor as a miniature sacred landscape in which rocky or mountainous formations support sacred trees, altars, architectural elements, and human figures, arguing that the primary focus is the sacred place itself rather than a specific narrated event. 

Within this framework the ring is treated as part of the Late Bronze Age Aegean glyptic tradition rather than as an isolated object. Vlachopoulos and other contributors to the ICON volume discuss it alongside rings such as the Isopata ring as examples of complex religious compositions built from recurring motifs like goddess-and-tree, epiphany, and guardian-animal scenes. Cain, analysing epiphany imagery, uses the Ring of Nestor and the Isopata ring together to illustrate how multiple ritual scenes can be juxtaposed on a single bezel without forming a linear narrative, and advocates reading the composition as a cluster of ritual images rather than as a continuous story. 

## Interpretation

Evans interpreted the Ring of Nestor as providing “a glimpse into the Minoan after-world” and framed the Thisbê treasure as evidence for Minoan funerary beliefs. In his 1925 publication he coined the name “Ring of Nestor,” explicitly linking the object and its imagery to the Homeric king of Pylos and to the broader Homeric world, even though he did not present any inscription naming Nestor. He read the ring’s imagery in terms of a world tree connecting cosmic zones, birds representing souls, and a guardian creature analogous to a dragon or tomb guardian, constructing an underworld narrative around the scene. 

Later iconographic studies have moved away from Evans’s detailed afterworld narrative and Homeric associations. The ASAtene article “Some observations on the iconography of the ‘Ring of Nestor’” analyses the ring’s imagery through internal Aegean comparanda, focusing on features such as the female figure, sacred tree, rocks, altars, architectural elements, and griffins. It emphasizes motif parallels with other Late Minoan I gold rings and wall paintings and does not regard the scene as a direct illustration of specific Homeric episodes or as the personal property of the Homeric Nestor. The authors raise the question of whether the bezel depicts a single coherent narrative event or a montage of standard cult motifs and express scepticism toward tightly constructed narrative readings. 

Vlachopoulos interprets the ring’s engraved scene as a religious composition involving a guardian figure protecting a sacred or world tree and compares the arrangement of tree, goddess, and guardian animal with similar compositions on Minoan and Mycenaean seals that have been understood as epiphany or underworld scenes. He regards the imagery as a complex religious composition built around core symbols—sacred mountain, sacred tree, divinity, ship, and winged creatures—belonging to an Aegean iconographic system of miniature sacred sites rather than as a continuous narrative. 

Cain uses the Ring of Nestor as a case study in the risks of over-interpretation. He argues that scholars from Evans onward have constructed elaborate epiphany and afterlife narratives for the ring by drawing on motifs such as the female figure, tree, birds, and guardian animal and by importing ideas from Homeric and later Greek texts. In Cain’s view interpretations that posit detailed journeys to the underworld or specific divine apparitions go beyond what the imagery warrants; he recommends treating the ring’s motifs as part of a wider set of Aegean religious symbols and cautions against close correlation with particular Homeric characters or stories. 

Cathy Gere highlights Evans’s reading of a butterfly or chrysalis-like element on the ring as an early manifestation of the Greek psyche (soul/butterfly) motif, noting that he used this detail to connect the ring to narratives about the origin of soul symbolism in art and psychology. She criticizes the practice of labelling Minoan and Mycenaean artifacts with Homeric names such as Nestor and interpreting their imagery through Homeric lenses, presenting the Nestor attribution as a product of early twentieth-century imagination rather than as evidence-based identification. 

The ICON volume and related studies on miniature sacred landscapes stress a methodological focus on internal Aegean iconography. Contributions position the Ring of Nestor among key seal images studied for their combinations of epiphany, goddess-and-tree, and guardian-animal motifs and explicitly state that its conventional name does not imply acceptance of Evans’s Homeric identification. Within this approach the ring is valued as a rich example of Late Bronze Age Aegean religious imagery rather than as direct evidence for Homeric characters or narratives. 

## Scholarly debate and authenticity

From the early twentieth century the Ring of Nestor has been the subject of authenticity debates. An article in the Journal of Ancient Egyptian Interconnections describes the “so-called Nestor Ring” as a pseudo-Minoan object with Egyptian-influenced iconography, noting that it was found in 1924, accepted as authentic by Evans, but condemned as a forgery by many other scholars. The study labels the ring “pseudo-Minoan,” placing it among objects that imitate Minoan style and lack secure provenance, and emphasizes that discussions of its origin have relied on contested narratives rather than on excavation data. 

Sakellarakis’s 1971 study, as summarized in later iconographic work, defended the ring’s authenticity primarily on iconographic grounds, arguing that motifs such as butterflies and a griffin supported an Aegean Bronze Age origin. Subsequent iconographic analyses review the authenticity debate, including proposals that link the ring to the circle of restorers and copyists Gilliéron and those that accept it as ancient, and stress that the object’s provenance is insecure and relies on narrative reports rather than excavation documentation. 

A 1998 technical study by Ingo Pini presents new observations that, in his view, support the ring’s authenticity. The article argues that the ring’s manufacturing and stylistic details align with known Minoan–Mycenaean goldwork and that these features reinforce its interpretation as an ancient object rather than a modern forgery. Pini treats the ring as having problematic or uncertain provenance, summarizing earlier discovery stories but concentrating on technical analysis rather than endorsing any specific findspot. 

A separate technical study accessible via ResearchGate reports “new technical observations” that “serve to support the authenticity of the Ring of Nestor” and notes that in 1995 the ring was once again placed on display at the Ashmolean Museum, indicating that the museum’s presentation of the object has been informed by such reassessments. A Cambridge synthesis on the art and archaeology of the Aegean Bronze Age states that, although the Ring of Nestor is considered authentic in that volume, doubts about it have not ceased and probably never will, characterizing it as a classic dubitandum. 

Vlachopoulos reviews earlier accusations that the Ring of Nestor was a pseudo-Minoan forgery and cites recent microscopic and metallurgical analyses, as well as iconographic parallels, to argue that it is a genuine Bronze Age Aegean gold signet ring. He concludes that the ring should be regarded as authentic and emphasizes its importance within the Late Minoan I glyptic corpus, while acknowledging that earlier doubts have shaped its historiography. 

Modern discussions distinguish between stylistic attribution and archaeological provenance. The Cambridge “Fakes and Dubitanda” chapter and Hudler’s study of gemmae dubitandae both note that the ring lacks secure archaeological provenance and must therefore be evaluated through stylistic and technical criteria rather than through stratigraphic context. At the same time, museum catalogues and scholarly analyses consistently describe it as a Minoan or Late Minoan I signet ring, underscoring a consensus that, despite ongoing reservations among some scholars, its style and construction fit within the Late Bronze Age Aegean glyptic tradition. 

Debate also surrounds the degree to which the ring’s imagery can sustain detailed narrative interpretations. Cain argues that readings which treat the ring as depicting a specific journey to the underworld or a precise mythic episode rely heavily on later literary sources and overlay more meaning than the minimal visual evidence requires, while other scholars, such as Vlachopoulos and the ASAtene authors, advocate interpretations focused on recurring religious motifs and miniature sacred landscapes. These differing approaches contribute to ongoing discussions about method in Aegean iconography and the limits of narrative reconstruction from seal images. 

## Later history and reception

The Ashmolean Museum’s catalogue identifies the object as a Late Minoan I gold signet ring and lists it under inventory number AN1938.1130, with the popular name “The Ring of Nestor.” Heritage Images and other derivative catalogues reproduce this description, referring to it as the “so-called ‘Ring of Nestor’” and noting four cult scenes on the bezel. 

A technical study reports that, following periods of doubt and re-evaluation, the Ring of Nestor was placed back on display at the Ashmolean Museum in 1995, after new observations were judged to support its authenticity. Subsequent scholarship has continued to cite the ring as an important, though contested, example of Late Minoan I glyptic art. 

The ring has played a notable role in modern cultural and scholarly narratives. Cathy Gere discusses it in the context of Evans’s broader influence on interpretations of Knossos and Minoan religion, highlighting how his reading of a butterfly-like element as an archetypal soul symbol fed into twentieth-century accounts of the psyche motif in art and psychology. The ring’s imagery and Evans’s interpretation have thus influenced not only Aegean archaeology but also modern discourse on symbolism and the reception of antiquity. 

Blog and popular accounts about Aegean archaeology, such as discussions of the so-called Griffin Warrior grave at Pylos, cite the Ring of Nestor as a famous example of Aegean religious iconography with unique compositional details. These treatments highlight its combination of motifs and its long-standing place in scholarly debates on Aegean seal imagery, but they do not present it as demonstrably belonging to the Homeric Nestor. 

Social media and image-sharing platforms circulate photographs and brief descriptions of the ring, often repeating that it is a Late Minoan gold signet ring now in the Ashmolean Museum and sometimes asserting a Cretan origin. Such posts contribute to the ring’s wider public visibility but generally do not engage with scholarly debates about provenance, authenticity, or interpretation. 

## Name and historiographical issues

Specialists emphasize that the label “Ring of Nestor” is a modern conventional name rather than a designation based on inscriptional evidence. Vlachopoulos notes that neither the reported find story nor the ring’s imagery supplies a personal name such as Nestor and that the label originates with Evans’s Homeric interpretation. He rejects attempts to identify the ring as the personal ring of the Homeric or mythological Nestor and treats the Nestor label as an interpretive tag rather than as evidence for ownership. 

Cain and contributors to the ICON volume similarly caution against reading the ring through Homeric narratives, arguing that the chronological gap and lack of textual or inscriptional linkage make direct identification with Homeric characters speculative. Gere explicitly critiques Evans’s practice of assigning Homeric names such as Nestor to Minoan and Mycenaean artifacts and regards the Nestor attribution as a product of early twentieth-century imagination. Modern scholarship therefore treats “Ring of Nestor” as a convenient shorthand for a particular Late Minoan I gold signet ring in the Ashmolean Museum rather than as an indication of historical ownership. 

## Notes on evidence conflicts

Published measurements of the ring’s bezel differ slightly: Ashmolean and CMS-derived data give approximately 3.29 × 2.18 cm, whereas Pini records a long axis of 3.27 cm, both indicating a length of about 3.3 cm despite the minor discrepancy. 

Date ranges assigned to the ring also vary: Pini’s Late Minoan IB–II range (c. 1530–1400 BC) is narrower than the wider Late Minoan or Late Minoan I ranges of roughly 1700–1450 or 1600–1450 BC found in secondary summaries and heritage catalogues. 

There is also a divergence between Evans’s presentation of the ring as part of a sepulchral treasure from Thisbê in Boeotia, later descriptions that associate it with Pylos or a tholos tomb at Kakovatos, and popular statements that describe it as “from Crete.” Modern dubitanda scholarship, however, treats all of these Boeotian, Pylian, and Cretan attributions as unverified narratives and maintains that the ring lacks secure archaeological provenance. 

Interpretations of the ring’s imagery differ in how much symbolic and narrative meaning they ascribe. Evans and later writers following his lead read elements such as the sacred tree, birds, guardian creature, and butterfly-like motif as explicit symbols of the soul and as parts of a structured afterlife narrative, whereas Cain, Vlachopoulos, and other iconographers argue that such detailed narrative readings extend beyond what the imagery securely supports and prefer more cautious interpretations grounded in internal Aegean comparanda. 

Earlier twentieth-century scholars often regarded the Ring of Nestor as a probable pseudo-Minoan forgery, while more recent technical and comparative studies by Pini and Vlachopoulos argue for its authenticity as a Bronze Age Aegean artifact, though general syntheses still classify it as a classic dubitandum whose authenticity debates are unlikely to disappear entirely.

## Abstract

The many years of research that led to the present paper on the so-called Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, nο. 277), with the documentation of its authenticity, have offered me the opportunity to discuss the cases of erroneous identifications of some Creto-Mycenaean gold rings as fakes . This tendency, underpinned by the obscure – even legendary – circumstances in which these rings were found, not only the Ring of Nestor but also the Ring of Minos, has been reassessed completely in favour of their authenticity. This revision has been significantly reinforced by recent finds of iconographic subjects of comparable resonance (wall-paintings, gold rings, figurines, ivories, and so on), as well as by more thorough study of the techniques and craftsmanship of these unique signet rings of the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age (16th-15th century BC). The key pictorial unit of the Ring of Nestor examined in this paper is Evans’s “watch-dog” or “dragon”, namely the guardian of the old “tree of the world”, whose branches host the most populous scene in Aegean glyptic art. This motif is here identified as a scorpion, a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Αge Aegean iconography, which kills the “Μinoan Dragon” of the ring and offers a sound interpretation of the ring’s iconography.

When Malcolm Wiener stated in his article that “jewelry above all is subject to the dictates of style and to the Versailles effect” (Wiener 1984, 24), he referred to the “Versailles effect” as an effect “most likely to occur where the cultural prestige of one society within an interconnecting set of societies is great” (Wiener 1984, 17). He pointed out that besides pottery ‒ frequently used for tracing movements of goods or even groups of people ‒ jewelry too has a high potential to illustrate intercultural patterns of commercial, political or ideological exchange. In doing so the “Versailles effect” does not implicate the simple imitation of the material culture of another, (dominant) culture by force or political /military domination, but rather describes a voluntary adaption to this culture, mostly expressed through art forms as well as pottery styles, architectural features or even technological inventions (Wiener 2016, 1-2). In this paper the focus will be laid on a quite similar effect here called the “Knossos effect”, made visible by an examination of distribution patterns of golden signets and their chronology. The term is a reference to Wiener’s term and is used here to describe a similar phenomenon “spreading” from the palace of Knossos in LM IA Crete.

This paper addresses the cultural translation of some exotica – selected valuable objects that were brought from the south Aegean or even more distant areas to Troy, Beşik-Tepe and Greek Macedonia mainly during the Late Bronze Age. The discussion will focus on jewellery and seals made of carnelian, steatite and bone. Such foreign goods, often labelled as imports, are usually objects with complicated histories. These histories began with acquisition, then went through various forms of ownership and display, and finally ended with release, all while simultaneously undergoing a process of domestication and 'de-exotification'. Release, especially an intentional release such as in the case of burial goods, treasures and cult deposits, is discussed comprehensively since these are the best-documented cases of interaction between things and people in the area of the north Aegean. Also discussed is the phenomenon of copying as a complicated procedure of appropriation, as well as the case of rejection of ornaments and symbolism.

[Helène Whittaker](https://gu-se.academia.edu/Hel%C3%A8neWhittaker)

In this paper I discuss the connection between the double axe and bulls. The double axe was undoubtedly one of the most important religious symbols in Minoan Crete. There is, however, no general consensus regarding its meaning. That the double axe was associated with the sacrifice of bulls and used to kill or to stun the animal was first suggested by Martin P. Nilsson in 1950 and probably still remains the most common interpretation, although perhaps more by default than for any other reasons. This interpretation is not implausible since the sacrifice of bulls would seem to have been part of Minoan ritual as documented by the iconographical evidence, most notably on the Ayia Triada Sarcophagus. Moreover, the figures carrying large double axes with a definite air of purpose that are depicted on a number of seals could plausibly be identified as sacrificial priests and priestesses (eg. CMS II.6, no.10). The interpretation of the double axe as a sacrificial implement has all the same been questioned, not least because we have no depictions showing it actually being used as such. The double axes depicted on the Ayia Triada Sarcophagus seem to be symbols rather than cult equipment, but this may be debatable. The iconographical evidence clearly indicates that there was some kind of symbolic connection between the double axe and bulls, whether this was related to sacrifice or not. Mention can be made of a number of seals which show a bull’s head with a double axe between the horns (eg. CMS II.3, no.11). The same motif also occurs on pottery. In most examples it is only the head of the animal which is depicted in connection with the double axe. The symbolic value of the double axe would seem to have been particularly associated with the head and perhaps specifically with the horns of the animal. It is noticeable that the horns can be shown in many different ways. The use of axes to shape the horns of cattle is widely attested in eastern African. The axes that are used in this process acquire exceptional symbolic value. This practice has an attested long time-depth and it is believed that it can be traced far back into prehistory and significantly in this context, it seems to be documented in ancient Egyptian iconography. That part of the symbolic meaning of the double axe in Minoan Crete could derive from its use in manipulating the horns of living bulls into a desirable shape is a possible interpretation of the iconographical evidence, which may also be supported by osteological evidence. In the last part of my paper I discuss the iconographical evidence for the association between bulls and double axes in terms of ritual meaning and cosmological beliefs.

What does the Ring of Nestor reveal about ancient Aegean gold craftsmanship?add

The study shows that the Ring of Nestor possesses 97% gold content, indicating high-quality Ancient Aegean craftsmanship comparable to notable pieces like the Archanes Ring and the Ring of Mycenae.

How does the Ring of Nestor's iconography compare to other Aegean artifacts?add

The Ring of Nestor features 14 human figures and several fantastic creatures, making it the most multi-figured among known Aegean signet rings, surpassing even the Ring of Tiryns and Ring of the Priestesses.

What techniques were employed in the creation of the Ring of Nestor?add

The bezel was crafted using traditional hand-chisel and hammer chisel techniques, with granulation identified as a critical aspect supporting its authenticity following experimental replication studies.

How did the Ring of Nestor acquire its contentious history of authenticity?add

Initially deemed a fake by scholars in the 1920s, ongoing debates around its authenticity involved notable figures like Gilliéron fils, who was suspected of crafting convincing forgeries, including backstories for his creations.

What cultural significance does the scorpion hold in the Ring of Nestor's imagery?add

The depiction of the scorpion at the tree's base serves as a guardian symbol in Aegean cosmology, reinforcing the narrative's themes of protection and the interplay between life and death in ritual contexts.

Post-doctoral Fellow at the University of Princeton (1998-1999) and Research Fellow at the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University (2001-2002). Undergraduate and postgraduate studies in Archaeology at the National and Κapodistrian University of Athens, specializing in Aegean Prehistory. My doctoral thesis (1995) negotiates the Late Mycenaean period on Naxos, for which research I received the Michael Ventris Memorial Award for Mycenaean Studies (1997). My main research interests are the Mycenaean period in the Cyclades and in Messenia, and the Aegean Bronze Age iconography (wall paintings, pictorial pottery, petroglyphs, seals). Collaborator in the Akrotiri Excavations, Thera, since 1989; director of the Kokkino Vouno, Akrotiri, Thera Archaeological Project (University of Ioannina) https://kokkino-vouno.project.uoi.gr/; director of the Vathy, Astypalaia Archaeological Project (Archaeological Society at Athens) https://vathy.project.uoi.gr/vathy_astypalaia_archaeological_project/ Since 2009 I teach Prehistoric Archaeology in the Department of History and Archaeology at the University of Ioannina; I have taught also at the universities of Athens (2006-2010) and of the Peloponnese (2004-2005), and have given lectures and seminars at universities in Europe, America and Canada. This paper focuses on a carnelian lentoid (M6621), housed in the Cabinet des Médailles of the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris, which was rejected as a forgery by Henri and Micheline van Effenterre when they compiled CMS IX (1972). The study presents a summary account of the collection's history, together with an assessment of the scholarly milieu in which the authors of the volume worked. There follows a detailed evaluation of the seal in question, in which material, shape, size, technique, composition, pose and style are all assessed. Comparisons are made with seals in circulation when the seal was acquired in 1907, as well as the repertoire known to the van Effenterres. These lead to the conclusion that the seal must be regarded as authentic, a view supported by recent discoveries. This case study thus helps to underscore the changing attitudes toward Aegean glyptic in the last century and the benefits we enjoy today with a substantial percentage of the extant repertoire now documented systematically in the CMS series, permitting comparisons to be drawn between pieces now widely dispersed. The opportunity of viewing images greatly enlarged on computer screens also facilitates the scrutiny of minute details that can lend weight in the rehabilitation of pieces previously regarded as suspect because they lack a secure provenance or have a murky past.

[Caroline J . Tully](https://unimelb.academia.edu/CarolineTully), [Sam Crooks](https://independentresearcher.academia.edu/SamCrooks)

The Bronze Age Aegean lacks a clearly discernible iconography of rulership, permitting widely contrasting speculation on the character of Minoan society; that it was egalitarian, heterarchical, gynocratic or a theocracy overseen by priest-kings. That elites did exist is amply attested through mortuary, iconographic and architectural evidence including the Throne Room of the Late Minoan palace at Knossos in which a centrally-oriented throne is incorporated into the architectural fabric of the room. Frescoes adorn the wall into which the throne is set, griffins flanking its large, mountain-shaped seat-back. Iconographic representations of human figures holding sceptres and standing upon mountains, and evidence for the increased palatial control of cultic activity at rural peak sanctuaries during the Neopalatial period (1750–1490 B.C.E.) emphasise an association between rulership and the mountainous landscape. Close analysis of seated figures within Minoan iconography reveals architectonic parallels to the Knossian Throne, stepped structures surmounted by seated female figures functioning as abstract representations of the mountain form. It will be argued that literal and metaphoric representations of a mountain throne function within an ideological program associating rulership with the natural landscape, offering new insights into the construction of power in the Aegean Bronze Age.----------- Paper presented at the 10th International Congress on the Archaeology of the Ancient Near East (ICAANE) on 27 April 2016.

## Extract

The first subject of the present communication is a truly royal treasure of gold rings and of bead-seals in the same metal found in a Mycenaean rock tomb near the site of Thisbê in Boeotia. The find was made in 1915, at a time when war conditions diverted the course of discovery from official channels, and a fortunate chain of circumstances now enables me not only to describe but to exhibit to the Society the whole hoard. Under the circumstances it is impossible without a breach of confidence to give all the details, but, from what I have been able to ascertain, the discovery was made by a peasant in a chamber-tomb excavated in the rock, by the village of Dombrena. Near this spot, about a quarter of an hour N.W. of Kakosi, on the Akropolis height of Thisbê, Mr. W. A. Heurtley, of the British School at Athens, kindly informs me that he was shown, in an olive grove, three chamber-tombs with _dromoi_. He adds, ‘The old man who showed me had dug one completely and found a dagger and vases and some sherds, all of which he had lost.’ Mr. Heurtley adds, however, that, from a drawing that the old man made of one of the vases, it is clear that it was a stirrup-vase of late type.

Other objects that I myself was able either to see or secure, found in the same group of tombs, but not authenticated as coming from the chamber containing the treasure, were bronze spear-heads and a short sword with the flange running round the extremity of the hilt, belonging to a very late Mycenaean type. A bronze razor also occurred of an advanced form and, of still later date presumably, a small perforated double-axe head of iron. There were also found a whole set of perforated glass-paste objects with holes below for the attachment of pendant gold disks which Mr. Wace has now conclusively shown to belong to necklaces. The particular type found, as well as certain paste pendants with reliefs covered with gold foil, belongs to the date of the Dimini jewels, or early L.M. III. _b_, in Minoan terms. There is no difficulty in ascribing the radiated glazed clay beads (Fig. 1, _a_) and the bugle bead of _kyanos_ blue paste (Fig. 1, _d_), as well as the plated faience plaques with groups of palms in relief (Fig. 1, _k_), to the same epoch.

page 45 note 4 Unfortunately in the recently published account of the investigations of the British School at Mycenae to which all are indebted for a rich accession of materials, including the most painstaking records and admirable plans (_B.S.A._, xxv.), the term ‘Helladic’—useful enough for the earlier periods—has been extended to include the Mycenaean Age. It starts from the assumption that the earlier phase at Mycenae represents the result not of actual conquest and the abrupt and wholesale displacement of a lower by an incomparably higher form of culture but of a gradual ‘Minoization’ of the native Helladic community. If this, as I believe, untenable position is given up, the whole _raison d'être_ for the term ‘Late Helladic’ ceases to exist. It is a great pity, indeed, that the name Mycenaean, which was already to hand and is generally intelligible, should be thus discarded.

 page 46 note 4b 

page 46 note 4b At the date when Minoan elements first impose themselves on the Peloponnese the predominant type of house belonged to the ‘apsidal’ class. This is seen at Tiryns, Korakou, and elsewhere in the stratum immediately preceding the ‘Mycenaean’ and seems to have been implanted there, in company with cist-graves containing contracted skeletons and bronze implements of peculiar type, by ‘Minyan’ intruders from North of the Gulf. The fixed hearth type of rectangular dwelling is common to both sides of the Aegean and, indeed, to late Neolithic Crete. But so far as the evidence goes, the Mycenaean type of Megaron shows most analogies with the Anatolian. Anyhow, it could not have been evolved _in situ_ from an antecedent type not to be found there in the preceding period.

## Summary

F orgers of antiquities have been active across all domains of archaeology ever since artefacts unearthed through excavation, whether legal or illegal, generated publicity and attained significant market value. This happened very rapidly in the case of Aegean art (H.-G. Buchholz, _Acta Praehistorica et Archaeologica_ 1, 113–35). Very shortly after Schliemann’s excavations at Mycenae, from 1883, reports appeared of a workshop making fake Mycenaean signet rings in the Peloponnese (Milchhöfer 1883, 59,n. 1). Evans’s work at Knossos from 1900 gave a major boost to the manufacture of fake Minoan antiquities.

Such discoveries took place in conditions especially favourable to forgery. The looting in Greece and Turkey of Hellenistic cemeteries at Tanagra (near Thebes in Boeotia) and at Myrina (near Izmir) released numerous terracotta figurines (the ‘Tanagras’) onto the market from the 1880s onwards. Several workshops made multiple copies, especially on Crete.

Ring of Nestor - A ~3700-year-old gold signet ring from Crete, Late Minoan Period, (c. 1700-1450 BCE), now housed at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford.

The authenticity of the Ring of Nestor is disputed.

It was first described by the archaeologist Arthur Evans in 1925. Its detailed design—featuring humans and mythical creatures—was interpreted by Evans as depicting religious scenes, possibly from the underworld, with links between Minoan civilization and Ancient Egypt. Some scholars argue it may be a modern forgery, possibly connected to Émile Gilliéron fils, an art restorer, suspected forger, and prolific collaborator of Evans's, in the ring's discovery.... while others support its authenticity based on wear patterns and technical analysis. Debate continues due to both stylistic similarities to genuine Minoan art and suspicious aspects of its discovery story.

## Summary

A long with frescoes, it is seals that best represent the Minoan art of this period: the richness of their iconographic repertoire is unmatched in the other arts. The growth in administrative activity entails an increase in their production; at Knossos, Zakros, and some villas like that of Haghia Triada this is reflected in the presence of archive deposits containing significant numbers of sealings. In total, nearly 2,000 seals and several hundred imprints allow for the study of Neopalatial glyptic – and this number is probably tiny compared to the total output. It has been estimated that at Knossos several thousand seals must have been in use at any one time (Krzyszkowska 2005, 119–53).

Ring of Nestor - A ~3700-year-old gold signet ring from Crete, Late Minoan Period, (c. 1700-1450 BCE), now housed at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford. 

The authenticity of the Ring of Nestor is disputed. 

It was first described by the archaeologist Arthur Evans in 1925. Its detailed design—featuring humans and mythical creatures—was interpreted by Evans as depicting religious scenes, possibly from the underworld, with links between Minoan civilization and Ancient Egypt. Some scholars argue it may be a modern forgery, possibly connected to Émile Gilliéron fils, an art restorer, suspected forger, and prolific collaborator of Evans's, in the ring's discovery.... while others support its authenticity based on wear patterns and technical analysis. Debate continues due to both stylistic similarities to genuine Minoan art and suspicious aspects of its discovery story.

## Abstract

![Image 10: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

This paper presents an analysis of the iconography surrounding the 'Ring of Nestor' in the context of Aegean forgeries and authenticity debates. By revisiting key iconographic features and comparisons, the paper aims to contribute to the ongoing discourse regarding the ring's significance in Minoan and Mycenaean art. Observations draw upon historical scholarship and recent discoveries to question and affirm previous conclusions related to the ring's motifs and their implications.

![Image 11: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

1.   The text explores the authenticity of the 'Ring of Nestor' through iconographic analysis.
2.   Contradictions in technical analysis highlight the importance of iconography in Aegean studies.
3.   The connection between incurved altars and the ring's depiction supports its authenticity.
4.   The ring's iconography may reflect cultural practices from the 1920s.
5.   Generations of scholars have debated the genuineness of both Nestor's and Minos' rings.

## Related papers

[Towards a Consideration of Unprovenanced Ancient and Medieval Finger Rings](https://www.academia.edu/37745254/Towards_a_Consideration_of_Unprovenanced_Ancient_and_Medieval_Finger_Rings)

[TN Pollio](https://independent.academia.edu/TNPollio)

This article will hopefully incentivize researchers to consider examining the untoward thousands of unprovenanced base metal and silver alloy finger rings being uncovered at sites from the U.K to Eurasia. Documented artifacts from controlled and stratified environments are of course essential towards understanding ring typology and routes of transmission across temporal and spatial environments. However, these standard methodologies should not preclude consideration of random and under-documented finds from non-professional sources. The rationale is simply that, within the last several decades, a significant proportion of new finds have in fact been made through amateur channels; and the rings they've uncovered may potentially contribute to our understanding of these underreported artifacts. Within the last few decades, the proliferation of metal detecting and use of the internet have ensured the issue is no longer of availability, but identity. The era of scarcity is obviously over, in view of the burgeoning array of base metal rings encountered on the international market. Any a priori disqualification of such a vast resource of emerging data is to ignore an untapped resource towards our understanding of ancient societies and the material culture associated therewith The need for reliable and broadly accessible reference material becomes increasingly apparent as more and more finger rings are uncovered and presented through on-line and other sources. Types which were once familiar only to academics have suddenly flooded the public conscience; but with little increase in resources towards the understanding of these artifacts. Small finds such as bronze finger rings are routinely uncovered at archaeological sites in Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Eurasia. They are typically noted in excavation reports, then cataloged and archived in places such as universities and museums. Unfortunately, both the reports and rings themselves are rarely accessible in mediums available to the general public. In most cases, only other professionals – such as academics and historians – are even aware of their existence. In terms of accessibility, most of this research has been compiled in unfamiliar languages and arcane formats which, to the general public, might as well be written in cuneiform and buried on the dark side of the moon. Many in English speaking countries have some proficiency in languages such as French, German and Spanish. But how many would understand technical reports written in Russian, Polish, Slovak, Bulgarian, Serbian, Romanian, Hungarian, Turkish or Greek – the languages in which much of this research has been published? Unfamiliar languages and limited/restricted formats are significant impediments toward the dissemination of this otherwise invaluable material.

Tο 2005 παραδόθηκε στο Αρχαιολογικό Μουσείο Θεσσαλονίκης ένα άγνωστης προέλευσης χρυσό δαχτυλίδι με έγγλυφη παράσταση ζευγαρώματος δύο τετράποδων (ΜΘ 23748), το οποίο παρέπεμπε εμφανώς στα κρητομυκηναϊκού τύπου χρυσά σφραγιστικά δαχτυλίδια. Η αναλυτική εξέτασή του έδειξε πως πρόκειται για πλαστό τέχνεργο, κατασκευασμένο στο τέλος του 19ου - αρχή 20ού αιώνα από έναν τεχνίτη με γνώση των δαχτυλιδιών και σφραγιδόλιθων της αιγαιακής Εποχής Χαλκού. Το δαχτυλίδι προσεγγίζεται εδώ ως ένα ιστορικό-πολιτιστικό τεκμήριο. Όχι, όμως, του μακρινού αρχαίου παρελθόντος από το οποίο υποτίθεται πως προέρχεται, αλλά του σύγχρονου κοινωνικού και πολιτιστικού περιβάλλοντος στο οποίο κατασκευάστηκε: ένα αντικείμενο εμπνευσμένο μεν από την αιγαιακή Εποχή Χαλκού, αλλά προορισμένο για σύγχρονη κατανάλωση. Ως τέτοιο ενσωματώνει το τι θεωρούνταν «Μινωικό»/«Μυκηναϊκό» από τον πλαστογράφο του και/ή τους υποψήφιους αγοραστές του, φανερώνοντας παράλληλα τις προκαταλήψεις, ανάγκες και επιθυμίες της εποχής που δημιουργήθηκε. Στο πλαίσιο αυτό επιχειρείται η ιχνηλάτηση των επιλογών του σύγχρονου πλαστογράφου, θέτοντας ερωτήματα, όπως: Πότε κατασκευάστηκε το δαχτυλίδι; Τι ενέπνευσε τον κατασκευαστή του; Ποιες ήταν οι επιλογές του -συνειδητές ή ασυνείδητες- όσον αφορά στο υλικό, την εικονογραφία, την τεχνοτροπία και την τεχνική κατασκευής και διακόσμησης του δαχτυλιδιού; Ποια στοιχεία του δαχτυλιδιού μάς φαίνονται ακόμα και σήμερα «Μινωικά»/«Μυκηναϊκά» και ποια φαντάζουν τελείως «λάθος» και μη πειστικά;

[One Ring to Know Them All: An Experimental Approach to Reconstructing the 'Ring of Hermes'](https://www.academia.edu/122737531/One_Ring_to_Know_Them_All_An_Experimental_Approach_to_Reconstructing_the_Ring_of_Hermes)

[Marios Koutsoukos](https://liverpool.academia.edu/MariosKoutsoukos)

Work In Progress, 2023

In Late Antiquity, no Roman would think twice about questioning the efficacy of ceremonial magic. They might doubt its legitimacy or, perhaps, the methods of the magician, but no one would ever dismiss magic itself as an operative force in the cosmos as well as a direct means of interacting with divine powers. Its potential efficacy was an accepted reality of life for layman and philosopher alike. It is in this cultural milieu that magical formularies such as those preserved in the Greek Magical Papyri circulated amongst ritual experts and Platonic philosophers with an affinity towards theurgy. What was the magical praxis like from the perspective of the operator? How did it enable a direct interaction with divine powers from a lived ancient religions point of view? When addressing these questions, modern scholarship very often confines itself in the traditional approach of textual examination, relying on individual accounts, such as that of the first-century Greek physician Thessalos of Tralles. or second-hand narratives, like those in Porphyry’s Life of Plotinus. The present paper proposes a hybrid method of studying Late Antique magical formularies which combines the methodology of textual approach with that of experimental archaeology. Termed experimental ritualism, this approach is presented through an experiment in reconstructing the magic ‘Ring of Hermes’ (PGM 213-303). This paper uses self-reflection to trace the process from the construction of the physical object itself to its ritual consecration and the attempts at putting the ring to its intended use. In effect, it is not merely the record of an experimental reconstruction but also an attempt at empirically adopting as emic a perspective as possible towards Late Antique magic praxis. Keywords: Graeco-Egyptian Magic; Greek Magical Papyri; Late Antiquity; Experimental Archaeology; Theurgy; Magic Ring.

The task of attributing seals to different hands or workshops is still a desideratum in Aegean studies, for the identification of Aegean seal-engravers and goldsmiths and their stylistic output could dramatically change our knowledge of the use, circulation and social impact of certain seals or seal groups and refine our methods of dating this (often only roughly datable) medium. A set of new data and methods now available, such as precise measurements of sizes and weights, x-ray analysis and material analysis finally enable us to shed new light on several questions concerning individual styles and thus to identify " masters " without the usual reliance on iconography. In this article, a set of thirteen signets will be presented in a detailed study highlighting their find contexts, their technical criteria and their iconographical similarities, leading to the conclusion that the rings were very probably made by six different " masters " working in the phases LH II – LH IIIA on Crete and the Greek mainland.

Jerusalem Journal of Archaeology

This paper presents a rare bronze finger ring that was found more than half a century ago and bears a symbol known mainly from the coins of Mattathias Antigonus. A teenager recovered it from one of the burial caves in the cliff of Naḥal David at ‘En Gedi. Although the cave was later excavated by Nahman Avigad, the ring was forgotten and was not incorporated in the excavation report. This paper discusses the ring, the symbol it bears, and its relation to the coins of Antigonus. I suggest a date and identification for the burials in the cave that associates them with the conflict between Herod and Antigonus.

What explains the authenticity debate surrounding the ring of Nestor?add

The research highlights that the ring's authenticity was primarily defended by Sakellarakis in 1971 due to iconographic elements like butterflies and griffin-headed women, despite earlier skepticism from many scholars.

How do incurved altars relate to the ring of Nestor's iconography?add

The study proposes that the platform depicted in the ring is supported by incurved altars, mirroring construction styles revealed by the Xeste 3 fresco, unknown to scholars until the 1970s.

When was the ring of Nestor first published and what was its initial reception?add

Published in 1925, the ring was initially viewed with skepticism regarding its authenticity, with many scholars attributing it to a forger's work due to perceived inconsistencies.

How did the research address previous skepticism about the ring of Nestor?add

The paper counters past arguments by demonstrating specific iconographic parallels, such as those identified in the Archanes excavation, revealing a strong cultural connection absent in forgery narratives.

What implications does the ring's iconography have for understanding ancient Aegean culture?add

The findings suggest a rich interplay between religious practices and artistic representations, as seen through elements like the lion, which may represent royal or divine power within ceremonial contexts.

Current Approaches and New Perspectives in Aegean Iconography, Aegis 18 (2020), pp. 223-252.](https://www.academia.edu/43416584/_2020_A_G_Vlachopoulos_The_Ring_of_Nestor_and_the_quest_for_authenticity_in_F_Blakolmer_ed_Current_Approaches_and_New_Perspectives_in_Aegean_Iconography_Aegis_18_2020_pp_223_252)

[Andreas Vlachopoulos](https://lastamp.academia.edu/AndreasVlachopoulos)

The many years of research that led to the present paper on the so-called Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, nο. 277), with the documentation of its authenticity, have offered me the opportunity to discuss the cases of erroneous identifications of some Creto-Mycenaean gold rings as fakes . This tendency, underpinned by the obscure – even legendary – circumstances in which these rings were found, not only the Ring of Nestor but also the Ring of Minos, has been reassessed completely in favour of their authenticity. This revision has been significantly reinforced by recent finds of iconographic subjects of comparable resonance (wall-paintings, gold rings, figurines, ivories, and so on), as well as by more thorough study of the techniques and craftsmanship of these unique signet rings of the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age (16th-15th century BC). The key pictorial unit of the Ring of Nestor examined in this paper is Evans’s “watch-dog” or “dragon”, namely the guardian of the old “tree of the world”, whose branches host the most populous scene in Aegean glyptic art. This motif is here identified as a scorpion, a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Αge Aegean iconography, which kills the “Μinoan Dragon” of the ring and offers a sound interpretation of the ring’s iconography.

[Sam Crooks](https://independentresearcher.academia.edu/SamCrooks), [Caroline J . Tully](https://unimelb.academia.edu/CarolineTully)

A group of Late Minoan signet rings fashioned in precious metals and engraved with complex and evocative iconographic schemes appears to depict ‘nature’ or ‘rural’ cults enacted at extra-urban sanctuaries, and may have functioned as inalienable possessions implicated in the expression and maintenance of elite identities during the Aegean Bronze Age. The images on the ring bezels depict human figures in association with epiphanic figures situated in settings characterised by the presence of trees and stones, columnar shrines, stepped altars, openwork platforms, tripartite shrines and sanctuary walls, perhaps involving occasional rites and the erection and dismantling of temporary cult structures which can themselves be viewed as architectonic replications of rural cult sites and natural forms. Just as the fabric of these rings and the artistry and technical skill of their production were of restricted accessibility and controlled distribution, we may infer that so, too, the rites, places and activities recorded on these rings were socially restricted. Possession of these distinctive and desirable objects of economic, cultural and symbolic value may have signified access to, involvement in and mastery over such rituals, the special status of the owner delineated and broadcast through the circulating media of clay sealings, advertising their special relationship with forces and places within nature. Over time the personal and cultural memory, knowledge and associations accumulated within these rings may form histories or biographies of the rings themselves, implicating the identities of their past and present owners, and of the wider community. In this way, they can be understood as inalienable possessions, objects invested with authority and authenticity that in turn authenticate the status of their owners. These enduring symbols draw the past into the present, instantiating cultural and cosmological ideals which classify and objectify social relations through referencing the past. Thus these rings function as mnemonic devices, palimpsests of memory, association and affect which store and transmit information about spatially and temporally disbursed places, people and events, memorialising and broadcasting elite association with the (super)natural world and forming part of the material affordances of the world of things which recursively produce, reiterate and transform identities through ecologies of practice: the past mediated in the present through memory materialised in objects.

INGO PINI

THE ‘RING OF NESTOR’

Summary.

In the past the authe ntic ity of the so-cal led Ring of Nes tor has been debated mostly in terms of iconography. Arguments against its ancient origin rest chiefly on the presence or absence of certain motifs elsewhere in the surviving repertoire. Most if not all of these arguments can be countered;an d we mu st re me mb e r th at ou r k no wl e dg e of M in oa n-M yc en a ea n iconography remains limited. Here new technical observations are presented which serve to support the authenticity of the Ring of Nestor. In 1995 the ring was once again placed on display in the Ashmolean Museum.
